content.text:
The image shows a benzene ring with four substituents.

Reading the ring from the top vertex and going clockwise:
- The top vertex is an unsubstituted CH.
- The upper right carbon carries NH2.
- The lower right carbon carries NH2.
- The bottom vertex is an unsubstituted CH.
- The lower left carbon carries F.
- The upper left carbon carries NO2.

The two NH2 groups are on adjacent carbons, so this is a 1,2-diamine. The NO2 and F groups are also adjacent to each other. The NO2 carbon sits next to the CH at the top, which is next to the upper NH2 carbon. The F carbon sits next to the CH at the bottom, which is next to the lower NH2 carbon.

Writing the SMILES: Nc1cc(N(=O)=O)... would use an unusual nitro form, so I use the charge-separated nitro group instead.

Starting at the upper NH2 carbon: c1(N) then c(N) for the lower NH2 carbon, then the CH at the bottom, then c(F), then c([N+](=O)[O-]), then the CH at the top, closing the ring.

SMILES: Nc1cc(F)c(cc1N)[N+](=O)[O-]

Checking this string atom by atom: c1(N) is the upper NH2 carbon. The next "c" is the CH, followed by c(F). Then c(...) carries the nitro group, written after the branch, and inside the branch "cc1N" gives the CH at the top and then the other NH2 carbon closing the ring. This puts the F carbon and the nitro carbon adjacent, with the CH between the nitro carbon and the NH2 carbon at the top, and the CH between the F carbon and the NH2 carbon at the bottom, which matches the drawing.

SMILES: Nc1cc(F)c([N+](=O)[O-])cc1N
